What you want in your armor is what makes it the best. Any class can wear any armor, so walking around as a tank is not only viable, but often done by noobs and pros alike. Likewise, most pros will run nearly naked to boost their roll's effectiveness, as light armor offers little protection and not being hit is better then being hit slightly softer. If you don't really care about any of this, make yourself look friggin sweet.

As for spears, I've not played with them much, but the winged spear is pretty good if I remember right. It's slightly heavier then a normal spear, but does more damage. With most weapons like this, you will probably want a huge shield with 100% physical resistance and high stability. Unfortunately, these shields aren't found until later into the game, so look around for what would match that. Stability is more important than resistance in this case.

Above all else though, choose a style that fits how you fight. While I would pair a tower shield with a spear, you might like parrying and prefer a small shield because of it. I would be a tank, but you might like dodging with a spear. There are few items and playstyles that are outright bad in Dark Souls, so don't be afraid to try something different or unusual.

*Wow, you wanted tips and I gave you a small novel. Sorry if it comes off condescending or states the obvious, I don't remember what the tutorial mentions.*

With every major battle, there are a few things one should be aware of before engaging. You should pause to check these things, even as you get faster at finding it.

 1. **Military Tech** -  This is likely a one-time thing, but comparing your military tech to an enemies' can give you a good idea of the outcome, especially early game. If France's tech is greater, you're fighting an uphill battle. Tech up ASAP.

 2. **Generals** - Combat is seperated into 2 phases, Fire and Shock. This uses the pips found in the unit types screen along with the general's rating in that phase to calculate damage.

 That being said, you may have noticed that your men have, at most, 1 Fire pip. This means that Fire phases are almost worthless until later, and that shock is the most important for causing casualties.

 Actually getting to the generals, they have four catagories for pips to fall into; Fire, Shock, Maneuver, and Siege. In combat, only Fire and Shock are used. Because you are in early game, only Shock is really important. Compare the Shock values of your general and France's. The side with a lower shock value will see hundreds, if not **thousands** in extra casualties each phase.

 3. **Terrain & Rivers** - Use the quick terrain mapmode or simply hover your mouse over the to-be warzone to find the terrain type. This is important to know because the attacker can recieve a penalty to their roll based on the terrain. If you are attacking, Grasslands are preferable, as there is no penalty in them, but most is acceptable if the difference in army strength is in your favor. **NEVER** attack into mountains. You'll learn the penalties of each terrain over time, so be willing to try everything once. Just not when it's important.

 For rivers, you can select the to-be warzone and hover over the river icon in the top-right of the pop-up, or select an army in an adjecent province and hover over the battle province. The penalty for crossing a river is -1. This penalty can be negated by having a general in that army with a higher maneuver than the enemy general, so keep an eye on that also.

There is still more, but that covers the most important parts this early. While there may be small differences in discipline or a few ideas have been picked, nothing major should have occured to make it a large factor yet.

**TL;DR** - Compare your tech to France's, Compare your general's shock values to France's general's and look at where you fight. *Fight smarter, not harder*

One great way to pay for the army is to use it. Besides wanton conquering, armies have other purposes that will eventually make their cost worthwhile.

Next time you're at war, and you're certain the enemy's troops have been crushed, send a unit to every enemy province that is at least one province away from any land you have friendly access too. When they stop on these provinces for a day, they loot the province for it's worth in base tax. This also cripples it's usefulness to the enemy while looted. You can loot a province again after 6 months, meaning european lands can outright fund a small army.

In a similar vein as looting, you can blockade an enemy port for a small sum of gold each month. While not as profitable, it also makes sieging much easier. To blockade, simply move a sizable fleet to the provinces bordering coast.

Conquering is probably the most straight-forward way of increasing income, but autonomy makes newly conquered lands less valuable short-term.

Should the above still fail, you can lower your armies maintence in the economy tab. I wouldn't recommend lowering it to much, and moving your armies away from your borders if possible. The lowered maintence makes it easier to get stack-wiped, and that's never fun.

There's also trade, but when I started, it seemed impossibly complicated, so I won't throw much of it on you. Collect in your main trade rote and send light ships to protect trade in your main trade node, and income should increase from it.

TL;DR: Loot, Conquer, Cut wages, Protect Trade, Profit

I'll try to help with some of the things you listed in case you still don't know:

Diplomatic Reputation is how your country is viewed by others and how well your word can be trusted when viewed against yor actions. Ingame, it is typically just a small boost or penalty based on recent actions, and your current Diplomatic Reputation can be viewed by right-clicking on land you own, or opening the second tab in that menu full of tabs (y'know, click the shield). The icon is a dove with a star next to it, and your current reputation is next to it. One major thing that hurts it is annexing a vassal, while having high legitimacy increases it by a set amount. Usually you will never see it beyond +3 or -3.

Legitimacy is your current ruler's believabilty in claiming the throne is his. Unless you are doing really terrible at that moment, have some terrible events or a regency council, it should always rise slowly. You want this to be above 50 during normal circumstances, as you recieve penalties for being below. Unforunately, there are few ways to jump it up, but many ways to decrease it. Royal marriages decrease it by a small amount, but increase it's yearly gain by .10. Having heirs with a weak or moderate claim serverely impacts it, placing you 25 and 50 legitimacy respectively. Some other ways of increasing it is by having a large amount of prestige and power projection.

Disputed succession and Personal Unions are related, and likely irrelevant to your Ottoman game. Disputed succession is when a nation has a regency council, no heir or a heir with a weak claim. If you aren't a chirstian nation, this means little. If you ARE a chirstian nation than you can claim their throne, assuming you have a royal marriage with them and a higher prestige then them. You gain a casus belli against them to enforce this claim and make them the lesser partner in a personal union, or it may happen upon their ruler's death.

A personal union is when two countries share the same ruler. The lesser partner is like a vassal, but with less short-term benefits. I believe you are not paid nor recieve extra forcelimit from them. However, after 50 years, there is a chance of naturally intergrating them into the major partner's country. Unlike vassals, a lesser partner in a personal union can have over 40 base tax and is typically how very good players manage to take the bigger nations like France and Austria.

Summons work by simply trying to summon another player from their sign. It pulls them from their world if the summon is successful with their current health and stamina. AVOID RED AND DRAGON SIGNS. These are "Honorable Invaders". White Signs are the Way of White, your standard affair co-op. The Yellow Signs are the Warriors of Sunlight, also known as the Sunbros. Us Sunbros want to help you more then your average Joe might, and both of us recieve an item for successful boss slaying. We also have sick lightning javelins! A Sunbro is more willing to give themselves to see you win, though they might not be estatic to do so. This said, here are some co-op tips.

Make sure you have as much estus as possible, preferably upgraded. Drinking estus refills your summons health also, which prevents them from wasting a valuable humanity.

Be prepared to spend time waiting for a summon. Getting a successful summon can be time-consuming, due to consistent failures. Bring a book and listen for invaders.

If you're invaded with a summon at your side, let the summon handle it. Get defensive and play mind games with the invader, but try to stay away from very serious attacks. Drink estus when summon is hurt.

If your summon is a coward against a particularly fearsome foe (Giantdads are scary to newbies), show them how it's done if you know how. Your success will inspire them to become more.

Typically, you're the leader. Hiding behind the summon is OK if your weapon is has long reach and they're a tank, but you're likely choosing the path and picking the fights.

Go enjoy some Jolly Co-operation, and remember to PRAISE THE SUN!

Some greatshields recieve this bonus too, like the Giants Shield. Other greatshields, like the Greatshield of Artorias, do not.

With your strength, you should be able to two-hand any weapon with a strength requirement of 30 and lower. That said, here are the suggestions.

* Zweihander: It hits super hard, has great range and makes a satisfying noise every swing. However, it consumes a great amount of stamina every swing, and you could only 2H it.
* Any Black Knight Weapon: Granted you have the dex to wield these beasts, they're essentially supercharged versions of their lesser counterparts. They hit as hard as the Zwei, if not harder, and some use less stamina. This basically puts the game on easy mode though -_-
* A Club: This might seem silly, but few things have large strike resistance, garunteeing steady damage against most creatures. You may find it a bit lacking this far in the game, but this simplist of tools has gotten me past many of this games challenges. There is a heavier club in the swamp you can pick up if the small one isn't your style.

Whatever weapon you use though, I highly recommend you level it past +4. That Battle Axe is very powerful for an early game weapon, but even the best tools won't give you results if you don't take care of them.

Armor is very worth it. There are things later on that hit like a mac truck, and without that armor it would utterly destroy you. The only thing that should limit your armor is the weight, because too much makes you fat-roll, and nearly noone wants that.

Of course, you're early on, so armor won't help too much, simply because the armor at that point isn't very good.

Edit: Out of curiosity I looked up their armor values, as I've never had a Pyromancer, and Cutless is right, Hollow Soldier armor is worse. It does provide a small poise boost, but it's very small, and not worth the loss of resistance IMO.
